# Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds

Jingwen Bai¹, Guochao Bai², Canbo Zhang¹, Shuangqi Li³, Minchao Hu³,
Weichun Huang², Shuang Liu^(1,∗)

¹Beijing Ou Rui Ling Shi Technology Co., Ltd.  
²ChangingTek Robotics Technology (Suzhou) Co., Ltd.  
³Shanghai Yunfan Intelligent Control Robot Technology Co., Ltd.  
^(∗)Corresponding author:
[shuang.liu@orillusion.com](mailto:shuang.liu@orillusion.com)

arXiv preprint – manuscript version 3.6 – 17 October 2026

Keywords: embodied agents, recursive self-improvement, robot
manipulation skills, portable skills, large language models,
verification, training-free adaptation, cost accounting

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Compile once, run cheap. Protocol A lets a strong author
generate, repair and qualify a skill offline; an independent gate
freezes it as an immutable FrozenSkill. Protocol B runs the same files
with executors that never see the skill code, on new layouts. Both
protocols share one non-bypassable runtime.

###### Abstract

Language models acquired agents, harnesses and reusable skills only
after data-rich pretraining had produced a strong base model. Embodied
intelligence has no comparable corpus, so current routes to new
manipulation capability either collect demonstrations for every task or
keep a frontier model in the control loop for every episode. We study a
third route: a strong general model acts only as an _offline author_
that writes, executes, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in
simulation until it passes a qualification exam on layouts drawn only
after freezing; the frozen skill is then executed by code alone or by an
inexpensive caller that reads nothing but its description, whereas
concurrent self-evolving systems still run a frontier model in every
episode at execution time. We call this skill-level recursive
self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol, with an
isolated and audited author, hidden validation layouts that are never
fed back, no-feedback and inherit-only control lineages and a
tamper-evident ledger, and a reuse protocol that runs the identical
frozen files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0
tasks with cluttered tables, 4 tasks were compiled into 7 frozen skills
by Claude Code; 5 of the 7 came from a first draft that already met the
targets and needed only qualification, at \$4.29–8.22 of author cost
each (\$55 per frozen skill once the 13 campaigns that did not compile
are counted). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns,
including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered experiment with 150
development layouts: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78–95 of
100 but had 3–16 safety aborts, so the pre-registered gate of 95%
success with zero aborts was not met, and a 100-episode exam bounds an
abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, a repair session that
inherits the previous version and its evidence delivered a better
version than a from-scratch rewrite in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign
test $`p=0.004`$; the selection-matched best-of-$`k`$ comparison is
5–3), and an inherit-only lineage, which revises the previous version
with its own practice runs but without the runtime’s development-layout
feedback, shows that most of that gap comes from inheriting the previous
version, with the development feedback adding a little more (3 of 3
campaigns in the same direction, $`p=0.125`$). Six write-once campaigns
found no detectable first-draft difference from practice, within a
design that cannot exclude effects below about 14 points. The frozen
skills measured for reuse retained 148/150 successes on new layouts with
no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at \$0.00028–0.00054
of model cost per episode; no direct-control baseline was run, so no
break-even is reported.

## 1 Introduction

The capabilities that make language models useful as agents were built
in a fixed order. Web-scale pretraining produced a strong base model
first; agent loops, tool harnesses, reusable skills and protocols for
calling them came afterwards, on top of that model. Embodied
intelligence is trying to repeat the first step and has no corpus with
which to do it. Robot foundation policies consolidate demonstrations,
but each new task still asks for new demonstrations or
post-training \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3)\]. A
second route places a frontier multimodal model inside a structured
harness and lets it reason per episode; it solves tasks zero-shot but
keeps the expensive model in the loop for every
execution \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6),
[7](#bib.bib7)\]. A third route lets a frozen model evolve skills,
critics or code through execution and revision \[[8](#bib.bib8),
[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10), [11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12),
[13](#bib.bib13)\].

The third route produces a loop; it does not yet say what kind of object
the loop produces or how its claims should be tested. Prior and
concurrent systems have begun to evaluate frozen experience on scenes
the loop did not see \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15)\], but at
execution time each episode still runs a frontier model, at a few
dollars per episode where the cost is reported \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], and
neither of these systems separates learning from feedback from selection
among attempts with a control. Three questions follow. First, can the
product of the loop run without the model that wrote it, and with what
loss when a cheaper model from another family calls it? Second, how much
of the improvement across rounds is learning from feedback, how much is
inheriting a previous version, and how much is trying several times and
keeping the best? Third, what does the skill cost, counted as the full
ledger of authoring, failed candidates, simulation and deployment, so
that the claim that a skill is cheap has a denominator?

We take the position that the order of the language-model history can be
inverted for robots: skills can come before the strong embodied base
model, be compiled by a strong general model that already exists, and
let robots start working, and generating structured data, in specific
scenes now. This is a hypothesis, not a result. Its necessary
precondition is empirical: a skill must be compiled cheaply enough,
qualify on unseen layouts, run without the author, and cost little per
episode. This paper tests that precondition.

Skill-RSI separates authoring from execution
([Figure 1](#S0.F1 "In Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
In Protocol A a strong model, whose weights never change, acts as an
offline author: it drafts a skill package from a task card, runs it on
fixed development layouts, reads the execution evidence, and revises,
until the package meets a target on those layouts and on hidden
validation layouts whose results it never sees. A qualification exam on
layouts drawn only after freezing decides whether the package becomes a
FrozenSkill, an immutable bundle of a skill description,
restricted-Python skill code, a perception module and a manifest with
hashes, seeds, environment fingerprint and compile cost. In Protocol B
the same bundle is executed by a code-only runner and by a caller from
another model family that reads only the skill description, on layouts
disjoint from every compile-time seed. We ask:

Q1  
How many repair rounds and how much author cost does it take to compile
a task to a $`95\%`$ qualification bar with zero unsafe motions, and
what stops the tasks that do not compile?

Q2  
Is the improvement across rounds learning from feedback, or selection
among independent attempts; within a repair round, how much comes from
inheriting the previous version and how much from reading its execution
evidence; and does the author’s own testing within a session contribute?

Q3  
When the frozen skill is executed by code alone or by a low-cost caller
from another model family, how much success is retained?

Q4  
What does a frozen skill cost per episode, with compilation amortized
over deployments?

Our contributions are: (i) an author–executor separation in which the
unit of adaptation is a verified, portable FrozenSkill that executes
with no model at all or with a cheap caller from another family, with
two protocols that operationalize compile-once-run-cheap; (ii) a
credible measurement of what self-improvement contributes: an isolated
and audited author, hidden validation layouts, exam layouts drawn after
freezing and run to completion, no-feedback and inherit-only control
lineages re-run on hidden layouts under a pre-registered design, and a
per-decision cost ledger that includes every failed campaign; and
(iii) measurements on RoboTwin 2.0 with two author products that answer
Q1–Q4, including three findings we did not anticipate: the frozen skills
came mostly from first drafts, so the protocol’s measured contribution
on the tasks that compiled is qualification and freezing; the gate binds
on rare safety aborts rather than on task completion, and more
development layouts did not change that; and most of the per-round
advantage of repair over rewriting comes from inheriting the previous
version rather than from the runtime’s development-layout feedback on
it, while in-session self-testing shows no detectable effect on first
drafts. We use the name Skill-RSI because the author recursively refines
a persistent external skill from that skill’s own execution evidence;
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not ‣ 3 Setting and Terminology ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
states precisely what is and is not claimed under that name.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Improvement in weight space

OpenVLA and later generalist policies map vision and language to actions
through learned parameters \[[1](#bib.bib1)\]; $`\pi_{0.7}`$ extends
this view with steerable, context-conditioned
behavior \[[2](#bib.bib2)\]. Self-improvement in this family updates the
policy from experience: RoboCat and self-improving embodied foundation
models practice autonomously \[[16](#bib.bib16), [17](#bib.bib17)\];
SOAR lets foundation models propose and judge
practice \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]; PLD probes a VLA’s failure regions with
residual RL and distills recovery data back \[[19](#bib.bib19)\]; RISE
trains on imagined rollouts from a compositional world
model \[[20](#bib.bib20)\]; RECAP turns deployment experience into
advantage-conditioned updates of $`\pi^{*}_{0.6}`$ \[[3](#bib.bib3)\];
ENPIRE lets coding agents rewrite the training code itself on real
hardware \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]. World-action models couple prediction and
action for contact-rich control \[[22](#bib.bib22), [23](#bib.bib23)\].
These routes need demonstrations, on-robot experience or training
compute for every task. Skill-RSI holds all weights fixed and evolves an
external artifact; the comparison is weight-space adaptation versus
artifact-space adaptation, not learning versus no learning.

### 2.2 Frozen models in harnesses

Code as Policies, Inner Monologue, VoxPoser and ReKep showed that
language models can write executable control programs and use
feedback \[[24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26),
[27](#bib.bib27)\]; REFLECT summarizes experience for failure
explanation \[[28](#bib.bib28)\]. Recent harnesses put frozen models or
policies behind structured observation–action interfaces: Show-Harness
exposes discrete semantic actions to a VLM \[[4](#bib.bib4)\],
Harness VLA orchestrates frozen VLA primitives with
memory \[[29](#bib.bib29)\], Guava and hierarchical VLA agents study
which harness components matter \[[30](#bib.bib30), [31](#bib.bib31)\],
AgentSpec studies scaffold composition \[[32](#bib.bib32)\], and
EmbodiedSkills wraps VLA agents in skills defined as executable
contracts with pre- and post-checks \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]. FAEA applies a
software-engineering agent to manipulation without
demonstrations \[[5](#bib.bib5)\], RoboDawn transfers VLM competence to
RoboTwin 2.0 control zero-shot \[[6](#bib.bib6)\], and RoboICL adapts a
frontier model to bimanual tasks from a few in-context
demonstrations \[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. The clearest statement of the
per-episode route is the early evaluation of GPT-6 Astra as a policy:
given RGB views, robot state and a task recipe, with no depth and no
privileged pose, the model chooses end-effector targets turn by turn and
reaches 22.5% success over 2,100 trials on the 42 RoboDojo tasks, far
ahead of two other language models used the same
way \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. In all of these the model reasons during
execution. Our runtime design follows theirs; our question is whether
the reasoning can be done once, offline, and its result handed to
something cheaper.

### 2.3 Self-evolving skills

Voyager grew a code skill library in an open-ended digital
world \[[35](#bib.bib35)\]. Embodied systems now close the
execute–diagnose–revise loop around frozen models
([Table 1](#S2.T1 "In 2.3 Self-evolving skills ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
RoboRSI coordinates Manager, Planner, Engineer and Reviewer agents over
a skill tree and consolidates stable tool-call chains into
code \[[8](#bib.bib8)\]; Zetta evolves runtime critics and recovery
skills around a frozen policy \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]; SHAPER evolves skills
and context-code harnesses with one frozen model as planner and
optimizer \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]; ASPIRE refines code-as-policy programs
into a library \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]; Playful Agentic Robot Learning
acquires skills through self-proposed play \[[12](#bib.bib12)\];
EmbodiSkill adds skill-aware reflection \[[36](#bib.bib36)\]; VASO
targets formally verifiable skills \[[37](#bib.bib37)\]; visual
verification steers policies at inference time \[[38](#bib.bib38)\];
Practice trains a skill learner that maintains a library for frozen
executors \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]; ELITE accumulates procedural strategies
for a frozen VLM and retrieves them by procedural
similarity \[[39](#bib.bib39)\]. SkillSmith and SkCC compile
software-agent skills into typed runtime interfaces \[[40](#bib.bib40),
[41](#bib.bib41)\]. Two concurrent systems are closest to ours.
EmbodiedEvo lets a coding agent evolve reusable Skills and Lessons on
one playground scene of each RoboDojo task, freezes them, and evaluates
on new scenes, raising a matched-test success rate from 8.50% to 30.17%
and transferring the experience to two other models (+8.86 and +5.50
points); at test time a GPT-6 Astra agent still reasons in every episode
with that experience as context, with up to 100 accepted code executions
per episode (29.0 on average with Skills and Lessons), at a mean
model-API cost of \$5.73 per test episode, excluding the playground
learning phase \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. EmbodiedRSI is an agentic harness
that adapts around the robot model: it co-evolves code and skills, holds
competing hypotheses in a graph, chooses the physical experiments that
discriminate between them, and reports 77.0% on RoboCasa365, 86.8% on
LIBERO-Pro and 71.3% on a real robot \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. Both evaluate
frozen experience beyond the scenes it was learned on; neither measures
execution without a large model, and neither includes a control that
separates learning from selection. Our difference from them is in those
two measurements, not in the loop. The repair loop itself has
antecedents outside robotics: Reflexion and Self-Refine revise an answer
from verbal feedback \[[42](#bib.bib42), [43](#bib.bib43)\], Eureka
refines reward code from execution statistics in robot simulation and
compares against sampling more candidates \[[44](#bib.bib44)\], and two
audits found that self-repair of code pays only when external execution
feedback is strong and that models do not improve their own reasoning
without it \[[45](#bib.bib45), [46](#bib.bib46)\]; our write-once and
inherit-only results
([Sections 7.3](#S7.SS3 "7.3 Q2a: in-session self-testing shows no detectable effect ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
and [7.4](#S7.SS4 "7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"))
replicate that pattern in the embodied setting. Skill-RSI could wrap any
of these systems as its author. Its requirements are on the output and
the evidence: an immutable package with a manifest, a gate between
discovery and release, execution of the identical package by an executor
from another model family, and a control that separates learning from
selection.

### 2.4 Recursive self-improvement as a term

The term goes back to Good’s ultraintelligent
machine \[[48](#bib.bib48)\] and Schmidhuber’s Gödel machine, which
rewrites its own code under proof \[[49](#bib.bib49)\]; STOP and the
Darwin Gödel Machine brought it to frozen language models that improve
an external scaffold or agent code against held-out
tasks \[[50](#bib.bib50), [51](#bib.bib51)\]. Duan et al. order
recursive self-improvement into five levels, from executing improvements
to improving the improvement process itself, and name embodied
intelligence as an application \[[52](#bib.bib52)\]. Surveys of
self-evolving embodied AI and post-deployment humanoid self-improvement
describe memory, task, environment, embodiment and model self-evolution
with a slow outer loop \[[53](#bib.bib53), [54](#bib.bib54)\]. In
software agents the term is now used for loops that improve an external
artifact while the model stays frozen: RRSI regularizes recursive
improvement of prompts, control flow, tools and memory so that reusable
mechanisms win over benchmark-specific ones \[[55](#bib.bib55)\]; AIDE²
lets an outer agent rewrite the harness of an inner research agent and
keeps changes that survive held-out benchmarks \[[56](#bib.bib56)\];
MetaSkill-Evolve evolves task skills on a fast loop and a meta-skill on
a slow one \[[57](#bib.bib57)\]; RSIAgent builds environment memory by
exploration without parameter updates \[[58](#bib.bib58)\]. In embodied
systems the term is now used concurrently by several groups: EmbodiedRSI
for hypothesis-guided co-evolution of code and skills in a harness
around the robot model \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], and PhysicalRSI, a preview
release without a paper, for a propose–evaluate–select–inherit loop over
a harness, skills and memory \[[47](#bib.bib47)\]. Our loop uses the
term in the artifact-level sense, sits at the first three of Duan et
al.’s levels, does not claim the fifth, and calls a gain
self-improvement only where a control lineage shows what the gain is
relative to;
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not ‣ 3 Setting and Terminology ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
makes the boundary explicit.

### 2.5 Hidden physical properties and touch

Text corpora contain almost no quantitative tactile knowledge, and touch
data are scarce; Sparsh learns touch representations from tactile
sensors \[[59](#bib.bib59)\], TacGen synthesizes tactile latents from
RGB to mitigate the scarcity \[[60](#bib.bib60)\], and DeliGrasp asks an
LLM to infer mass, friction and compliance from object semantics to set
grasp forces \[[61](#bib.bib61)\]. These works complete the missing
modality. Our route is complementary: a skill can encode a strategy that
avoids needing the modality, such as supporting a fragile object from
below rather than estimating a safe grip force;
[Section 8](#S8 "8 Discussion ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
discusses where that substitution stops working.

### 2.6 Evaluation validity

LIBERO measures lifelong transfer \[[62](#bib.bib62)\]; LIBERO-PRO and
LIBERO-Plus expose memorization and decompose robustness into
perturbation dimensions \[[63](#bib.bib63), [64](#bib.bib64)\];
RoboTwin 2.0 provides domain-randomized bimanual tasks and a public
expert generator \[[65](#bib.bib65)\]; VLABench, ESI-Bench and
BEHAVIOR-1K extend scope \[[66](#bib.bib66), [67](#bib.bib67),
[68](#bib.bib68)\]. Recent audits find shortcuts, repeated test exposure
and low trial counts behind reported progress \[[69](#bib.bib69)\], and
cost-controlled evaluation of agents asks that accuracy be reported with
the dollars spent to reach it \[[70](#bib.bib70)\]. These concerns apply
with particular force to self-evolving systems, whose tasks are also
their discovery set, and to agentic authors with shell access, which, we
found, read other campaigns’ work when nothing stops them
([Section 4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px8 "Author isolation and audit. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
We respond with author isolation and session audits, hidden validation
layouts, exams drawn after freezing, run-to-completion exams, seeds
disjoint across protocols, and a full ledger of failed candidates.

## 3 Setting and Terminology

### 3.1 Components

A task instance is a partially observed process in which a dual-arm
robot receives observations, executes primitive actions and transitions
under simulator dynamics. Skills do not emit joint torques. A fixed
_kernel_ exposes six primitives
([Table 11](#A1.T11 "In Appendix A FrozenSkill Package and Primitive API ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"),
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A FrozenSkill Package and Primitive API ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")):
observe, ee_pose, gripper_state, move_pose, gripper and wait, and
translates them into planned trajectories under workspace, joint and
drop monitors with safety abort. The system has an _author_ $`A`$ (a
strong model product used only offline), an _executor_ $`E`$ (a
code-only runner or a caller model), the _skill package_ $`K`$, the
kernel $`D`$ and an _evaluator_ that reads privileged simulator state to
decide success. The author never reads the evaluator; the executor never
reads the skill code.

### 3.2 Compile–reuse boundary

We call the setting _target-task weight-update-free_: neither author nor
executor parameters change for the target task; no new human
teleoperation or expert trajectories are collected for it; simulation
rollouts, environment predicates, structured traces and the declared
primitive API may be used; the external skill may change during
compilation and never afterwards. Foundation-model pretraining is not
zero, simulator interactions are data and success predicates are
supervision, so we avoid the phrases “zero data” and “from scratch”. The
boundary between Protocol A and Protocol B is a hash: the three skill
files and the manifest are content-addressed at freezing, and every
reuse episode verifies them before execution.

### 3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not

Ordinary episode retry is not self-improvement, and a higher final score
alone does not show that a process improved itself. We use four stages
that match the released code. R0 generate: independent drafts of the
package from the task card. R1 repair: recursive refinement of a
persistent package, in which version $`k{+}1`$ is written by the author
from version $`k`$ and from the execution evidence of version $`k`$ on
the development layouts. R2 qualify: an exam on layouts drawn after the
package is frozen. R3 reuse: execution of the frozen package by
executors that did not author it. The recursion is over the artifact,
not over the author: the author’s weights, prompts, tools and diagnostic
procedure are fixed for the whole run, as in recent harness-level
recursive self-improvement for software agents \[[55](#bib.bib55),
[56](#bib.bib56)\]. In the five-level ordering of Duan et
al. \[[52](#bib.bib52)\], R1 exercises improvement execution, strategy
choice and experience acquisition, but not meta-level improvement of the
improver, which we leave to future work.

Two kinds of self-improvement occur in a campaign and we measure them
separately. _In-session_ improvement happens inside one author session:
the product writes, tests on practice layouts or in its own simulator
account, and revises before delivering; every R0 draft already contains
it. _Cross-session_ improvement is R1: each round is a new session that
inherits the package and the evidence of all earlier versions. We define
the _RSI delta_ of a campaign as exam success minus the
hidden-validation baseline of the selected R0 draft, which is the
cross-session part; the in-session part is the difference between that
baseline and the baseline of a _write-once_ draft produced under a
condition in which the author cannot run the package at all
([Section 4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px10 "Ablations and post-hoc evaluations. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
A repair round contains three separable ingredients: _selection_ (the
runtime keeps the best version), _inheritance_ (the author starts from
the previous version instead of from the task card) and _development
feedback_ (the author reads the runtime’s per-layout evaluation of the
previous version on the development block). All lineages keep the
author’s own practice runs on practice layouts, so what the control
lineages remove is not testing but the runtime’s evaluation. They remove
the ingredients one at a time under the same selection rule: a
no-feedback rewrite has neither inheritance nor development feedback, an
inherit-only lineage has inheritance without development feedback, and
repair has both; the differences repair$`-`$inherit, inherit$`-`$control
and repair$`-`$control therefore measure the marginal effect of the
development feedback, the effect of inheritance, and their sum. Claims
about “self-improvement” in this paper are claims about R1 and are
licensed only by those controls, evaluated on layouts that none of the
lineages has seen.

### 3.4 The FrozenSkill package

A package has four files. SKILL.md (at most 20 KB) starts with a front
matter naming the skill and its atoms and then documents each atom, a
standard flow and a recovery section; it is the only file a caller may
read. skills.py defines ATOMS, each atom as atom(api, args) -\> {ok,
...}, and fallback(api), a complete code-only policy. perception.py
defines detect(rgb, depth, calibration), which must return, from the
RGB-D image, exactly one component per task role (a pixel box, a world
position, a point count and any further numeric fields the author
chooses) plus a table-height estimate; a frozen CLIP model, fixed by the
runtime, scores the author’s crop boxes against the role names and
assigns the roles, and observe() hands the resulting components to the
skill. Perception is therefore the author’s, role naming is the
runtime’s. rationale.md records design decisions and is excluded from
the frozen bundle. Both Python files are _restricted Python_: no
imports, no while, try, classes or lambdas, a builtin allowlist, and no
underscore names; a static validator rejects anything else, and the
runtime enforces that skills touch the simulator only through the API.
The frozen bundle adds MANIFEST.json: file hashes, runtime version (the
API contract), environment fingerprint, gate outcome, the development,
validation, exam and caller-check seeds, and the compile-cost summary
([Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A FrozenSkill Package and Primitive API ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).

A package runs in two modes. In fallback mode fallback(api) runs alone;
no model is involved. In orchestrated mode a caller reads SKILL.md,
receives the task, one observation and the execution log so far, and
returns a plan of at most eight steps, each an atom call, an observation
or a state read; the runtime executes the plan, stops at the first
ok: false, and asks again, at most four times per episode during
compilation. The caller has no tools and cannot move the robot except
through atoms. Per-episode limits are 90 primitive calls, 90 simulated
seconds and 240 wall-clock seconds excluding caller latency. After the
skill returns, the robot holds still for two simulated seconds before
the official success predicate is read, so that an object released at
the last moment is judged where it comes to rest.

## 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill

Protocol A is a scripted coordinator that never calls a model for
judgement and never interprets results for the author. Its stages are
summarized in
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In Ablations and post-hoc evaluations. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds");
the parameters are in
[Table 12](#A2.T12 "In Appendix B Gate Parameters and Qualification Checklist ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
([Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Gate Parameters and Qualification Checklist ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).

#### Preparation and lock.

A task configuration names the instruction and the object roles;
everything else is generated from the official RoboTwin 2.0 source. The
task card given to the author contains the instruction, the roles, the
success predicate source, object generation parameters, one example
observation and the robot’s gripper calibration; the expert generator is
on a deny list and is never shown. All campaigns use one scene tier,
_clutter_: the official demo_clean configuration with up to ten
task-irrelevant distractor objects on the table (none in 2% of layouts),
fixed lighting and background, and no table-height randomization. A
phase-0 health check materializes 30 layouts, runs the official expert
ten times to confirm feasibility and to fix the speed bar, checks
reachability, and calibrates the gripper; it stops the campaign on red
lights (materialization failure above 10%, expert success below 30%, an
unreachable role, an inseparable gripper reading). The gate
specification (success bar, safety, speed factor, regression rule) is
written before any author session and never edited. Three seed blocks
are then materialized: 50 _development_ layouts (seeds 70000–70049), 50
_validation_ layouts (71000–71049) whose results are never shown to the
author, and a practice range (68000–68999). A layout that the official
scene generator fails to stabilize is dropped for every version, so the
usable blocks had 42–47 development and 36–46 validation layouts per
task; targets are stated as fractions of the usable block.

#### R0: independent drafts.

Two author sessions start in separate working directories with identical
inputs and write a first package each. Each package passes static
validation and runs in fallback mode on the development layouts. The
better draft (more successes; ties broken by fewer primitive calls)
becomes the lineage head; its directory, including the author’s own
notes, is copied into the repair workspace. Before any repair, the head
is run once on the validation layouts; this _validation baseline_ is the
“before” measurement for the whole campaign, because the development
score of a selected draft is biased upward by the selection itself.

#### R1: repair until target.

Each round starts a fresh author session of at most one hour in the
repair workspace. The author sees every earlier version, its per-layout
outcomes on the development layouts (success, failure class, call
counts, safety events, and for failed layouts the primitive trace and
observation fields), the verdict that compared it with the head, the
current head, and its own notes. It must deliver a complete package; the
runtime runs it in fallback mode on the development layouts and replaces
the head only if the new version has strictly more successes. When the
head reaches the development target ($`\geq 96\%`$ of usable layouts),
it is run once on the validation layouts; if it reaches the validation
target ($`\geq 94\%`$) R1 ends, otherwise the author is told only that
“the package did not yet meet the acceptance bar” and repair continues.
R1 also ends after ten rounds, after three consecutive rounds without
improvement, or when the author’s observable cost reaches \$150 or its
session time ten hours; in every case the campaign proceeds to R2, so
that each campaign ends with an exam.

#### Practice and the author’s own experiments.

The author may run up to 30 practice episodes per round on practice
seeds through a gateway, and, since runtime 5.5.0, holds an unprivileged
account on the simulation host where it can run its own experiments with
the installed simulator on a shared GPU slot. These are the means of
in-session improvement; both are logged, and any episode not scheduled
by the coordinator is listed as unscheduled.

#### Control lineages.

The replacement rule alone raises the head’s development score over
rounds even if the author learns nothing, because each round is another
draw on the same layouts. To separate learning from selection, when
repair round $`k`$ starts the coordinator also starts control draft
$`C.k`$: a new working directory with exactly the R0 inputs and prompt,
no history and no feedback, evaluated in fallback mode on the same
development layouts. Draft and control directories carry random names.
Two comparisons follow. The _best-of-$`k`$_ comparison, with $`r_{j}`$
and $`c_{j}`$ the fallback successes of repair $`j`$ and control $`j`$
on the development layouts and $`R_{0}`$ the set of R0 scores, is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{Learn}(k)=\max(R_{0}\cup\{r_{1}..r_{k}\})-\max(R_{0}\cup\{c_{1}..c_{k}\}),
``` |  | (1) |

which matches attempts and selection rule on both sides. The *per-round*
comparison asks whether the version delivered by repair round $`k`$ is
better than the version delivered by control draft $`k`$; because the
repair session has seen the development layouts and the control has not,
this comparison is made on the hidden validation layouts, on which every
$`R1.k`$ and $`C.k`$ is run once after the campaign ends (runtime 5.8.0;
report-only, never fed back). The two comparisons are not equivalent:
repair starts from the better of two drafts and keeps only strict
improvements, whereas each control is a single fresh draw, so the
per-round comparison also credits repair for not discarding an already
selected starting point; we therefore also report each lineage relative
to the campaign’s own starting point. The control was enabled on a
subset of campaigns because it costs one author session per repair
round.

A second experiment, pre-registered on 2026-10-10 before any of its
campaigns ran (runtime 5.9.0; registration text and deviation record in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Pre-registration of the Second Experiment and Deviation Record ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")),
adds a third lineage to separate inheritance from feedback. An
*inherit-only* lineage $`I.k`$ is copied from the R0 starting workspace
with the author’s notes and practice records kept and the starting
version’s feedback and verdict deleted; each round the author revises
the previous version with the same 30 practice episodes per round, whose
results it sees, but receives none of the runtime’s development-layout
evaluation (no per-layout outcomes, traces or verdicts of any version),
only whether the runtime replaced the head. Rounds are matched to the
repair lineage, the inherit-only author has its own host account, its
cost is not charged against the repair caps, and its versions are not
examined. The same experiment raised the development block from 50 to
150 seeds (70000–70149; 128 usable after materialization) on the task
that had never compiled, to test whether a block large enough to show a
1–3% abort rate lets repair clear the gate; the validation block, the
targets, the round and patience limits and the gate were unchanged. Its
primary outcome, fixed in advance, is the number of campaigns frozen out
of three, reported descriptively; its secondary outcomes are the RSI
delta and the abort count of each campaign, and the per-round held-out
comparisons repair$`-`$inherit, inherit$`-`$control and
repair$`-`$control with the campaign as the unit of the sign test, which
with three campaigns has a minimum attainable one-sided $`p`$ of 0.125.
The registration states that the two changes, more layouts and the new
lineage, were introduced together, so a change in the primary outcome
could not be attributed to either alone.

#### R2: qualification exam.

Before the exam the coordinator verifies the hash-chained ledger, the
runtime manifest and the official code tree; any change voids the
campaign. The head is frozen; only then are 100 exam seeds drawn
uniformly from $`[10^{5},10^{6})`$, disjoint from all earlier seeds. The
exam runs in fallback mode and passes if successes are at least 95 of
100, no *safety abort* occurs (an object dropped below the table plane,
an end effector leaving the workspace box, a joint beyond its limit, or
an invalid pose request; distractors are not monitored), the median
simulated time of successful episodes is at most twice the expert median
from phase 0, and the frozen version is not worse on the development
layouts than any version previously accepted as head. In every episode
of both protocols the official success predicate is evaluated only after
a 2 s settle in which the robot holds still while safety monitoring
continues (not counted against the time budget; the phase-0 expert is
judged the same way), so that an object released just before the check
cannot be judged while still moving. Failure is decided as soon as more
than five episodes have failed, but the exam always runs to completion
so that failed campaigns report a comparable success rate; the outcome
is frozen, failed exam (R1 reached its targets but the exam failed) or
not compiled (R1 ended on a budget rule). No retake is allowed. The rule
is a point-estimate threshold: a skill that passes with 95 of 100 has a
Wilson lower bound of only 88.8%, and $`n{=}100`$ was chosen so that the
interval at the threshold has a half-width of about 4.5 points, not so
that the bar is demonstrated with confidence; we report the interval
beside every verdict. A passing package is written as a FrozenSkill with
its manifest.

#### Caller check.

After freezing, the coordinator runs 20 episodes on fresh seeds in
orchestrated mode with the author product as caller, reading only
SKILL.md. The result does not affect the gate; it is recorded so that a
description that code can execute but callers cannot follow is detected
before Protocol B, with a warning if it falls more than 15 points below
the exam score.

#### Author isolation and audit.

The author runs with a shell, network access and a simulator account
because practice needs them. In an earlier version of the protocol
without isolation, an audit of 58 campaigns’ session transcripts found
that in five the author had read and copied skill code, notes or scores
of other campaigns on the same machine, and that one formal campaign’s
starting draft was 0.96 similar to an earlier candidate for the same
task and had been tested on hidden validation layouts; none of those
campaigns is reported here. Since runtime 5.5.0 the author process runs
in an OS sandbox restricted to its own working and home directories,
each working directory has its own unprivileged user and key on the
simulation host with a read-only view of its permitted files, validation
and exam layouts and other campaigns are unreadable, and every campaign
ends with an automatic audit that pairs each tool call in the session
transcripts with the result returned to the model. The audit grades a
campaign *clean*, *metadata* (another campaign’s identifier seen in a
directory or process listing, no content), *review* (a path of another
campaign appeared in a result; checked by hand, no content read),
*contaminated* (content of another campaign read) or *unaudited*
(transcripts missing); the last two invalidate the campaign.

#### Tamper evidence.

The results ledger is hash-chained, the runtime is pinned by a manifest
recorded at campaign creation, the official code tree is hashed, exam
seeds do not exist until freezing, and feedback generation asserts that
no validation or exam seed appears in what the author sees. Each
campaign records an environment fingerprint (GPU, driver, PyTorch,
planner build); campaigns with different fingerprints are never
compared, because planner numerics change outcomes on identical layouts.

#### Ablations and post-hoc evaluations.

Two ablation conditions stop after the validation baseline: *practice
only* removes the simulator account (runtime 5.6.0), and *write once*
removes practice as well, telling the author that the package cannot be
run before delivery (5.7.0); the task card and the rest of the prompt
are otherwise identical. Both conditions were added after the first
formal campaigns had run and their first-draft scores were known; they
were not pre-registered. Two report-only commands were added after the
first formal results and are not pre-registered: a *re-evaluation* of
the exam version on 300 further layouts drawn disjointly from all
earlier draws (5.5.3), and the *held-out* re-run of every repair and
control version on the validation layouts described above (5.8.0).
Neither changes any campaign outcome.

1: task card $`T`$, author $`A`$, dev seeds $`S_{d}`$, validation seeds
$`S_{v}`$, gate $`G`$ (locked)

2: $`K_{a},K_{b}\leftarrow A(T)`$ in separate directories
$`\triangleright`$ R0

3: head
$`\leftarrow\arg\max_{K\in\{K_{a},K_{b}\}}\mathrm{fallback}(K,S_{d})`$

4: $`b_{v}\leftarrow\mathrm{fallback}(\text{head},S_{v})`$
$`\triangleright`$ validation baseline, hidden

5: for $`k=1,2,\dots`$ until a stop rule fires do $`\triangleright`$ R1

6:   start control draft $`C.k\leftarrow A(T)`$ with no history
$`\triangleright`$ optional

7:   start inherit-only draft $`I.k\leftarrow A(I.{k-1})`$ without
development feedback $`\triangleright`$ second experiment

8:
  $`K_{k}\leftarrow A(\text{head},\text{evidence}(\cdot,S_{d}),\text{history})`$

9:   if
$`\mathrm{fallback}(K_{k},S_{d})>\mathrm{fallback}(\text{head},S_{d})`$
then head $`\leftarrow K_{k}`$   

10:   if $`\mathrm{fallback}(\text{head},S_{d})\geq 0.96|S_{d}|`$ and
$`\mathrm{fallback}(\text{head},S_{v})\geq 0.94|S_{v}|`$ then break   

11: verify ledger chain, runtime manifest, official tree; freeze head
$`\triangleright`$ R2

12: $`S_{e}\leftarrow`$ 100 seeds drawn now, disjoint from all prior
seeds

13: outcome
$`\leftarrow G(\mathrm{fallback}(\text{head},S_{e}),\text{aborts},\text{speed},\text{regr.})`$

14: if outcome = passed then write FrozenSkill with manifest; run caller
check

15: audit session transcripts; return outcome, compile cost, curves

Algorithm 1 Protocol A: compile one task with one author

## 5 Protocol B: Measuring Reuse

Protocol B takes a FrozenSkill and never modifies it. The version run
here is the minimal one implemented inside the compile runtime (5.8.0):
it verifies the three file hashes against the manifest, checks that the
runtime version and environment fingerprint match, draws 50 seeds from
the exam range excluding every development, validation, exam and
caller-check seed recorded in the manifest, and executes every arm on
the same 50 layouts.

#### Executor arms.

F runs fallback(api) with no model. O-ds is an orchestrated run with
deepseek-flash as caller, chosen because it is inexpensive, fast, and
from an organization different from the author’s; the caller sees only
SKILL.md, receives the identical prompt template used in the caller
check, and may decide up to twelve times per episode (the mean number of
decisions is reported). Decoding used temperature 0 with an output limit
of 32,768 tokens including reasoning (hosted decoding at temperature 0
is not bit-reproducible). A plan that fails to parse is an invalid
decision charged to the caller, not an infrastructure failure. We did
not run callers from further model families, a strong-model caller, or
the direct-online baselines of the full design
([Section 9](#S9 "9 Limitations and Safety ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).

#### Ledger.

Every decision records the arm, exact model identifier, UTC time, input,
cached and output tokens, the price applicable at that time, cost,
latency and the raw response; every episode records success, failure
class, safety events, decisions, primitive calls, simulated and
wall-clock time, and atom entry and exit marks. Costs are
provider-reported usage multiplied by the price captured on 2026-10-08
(peak or off-peak by UTC hour,
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Price Snapshot ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"));
unavailable usage is recorded as null, never estimated.

#### Statistics.

Success rates carry Wilson 95% intervals \[[71](#bib.bib71)\];
safety-abort rates carry Clopper–Pearson exact intervals. Counts pooled
over skills are sums and are labelled as such. Arms share seeds, so
paired tests are possible in principle; with the outcomes observed here
the number of discordant pairs is too small for any test to separate the
arms, and we report the counts. Per-episode cost with compilation
amortized over $`N`$ deployments is $`C/N+c_{X}`$, with $`C`$ the author
cost from the manifest and $`c_{X}`$ the arm’s mean model cost per
episode; simulation compute is listed but not priced.

## 6 Experimental Setup

#### Environment.

All experiments use RoboTwin 2.0 \[[65](#bib.bib65)\] with the
aloha-agilex dual-arm embodiment, the clutter tier described above, and
cuRobo-based planning behind the primitive API. The planner’s collision
world contains only a static table box ($`0.7\times 2\times 0.04`$ m)
and the robot’s self-collision; task objects and distractors are not in
it, so a planned arm trajectory avoids the table and the robot but not
the objects on the table, and keeping clear of them is the skill’s
responsibility through the poses it requests. Everything ran on one
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 (driver 595.71.05, PyTorch 2.8.0+cu128, OptiX
denoiser) with four concurrent simulator slots; the environment
fingerprint was identical for every campaign and evaluation reported
here. The compile runtime was frozen at version 5.5.0 before the first
formal campaign and received seven increments during the study
(5.5.1–5.8.0: sandbox and GPU-slot fixes, the report-only evaluations,
audit support for the second product, quota-exhaustion handling, and the
minimal reuse protocol), each dated in the released protocol; none
changed the default author prompt or a gate rule; the primary Claude
campaigns ran on 5.5.0–5.6.0, the GPT-6 campaigns on 5.6.1–5.8.0,
Protocol B on 5.8.0, and the pre-registered second experiment on 5.9.0,
which added the inherit-only lineage and the larger development block
and changed nothing else.

#### Tasks and campaigns.

Seven RoboTwin 2.0 tasks were compiled
([Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
They were chosen after piloting, not before. A pilot on the fully
randomized scene tier found first drafts above 82% on four tasks, so the
clutter tier was used throughout; pilots on the clutter tier from
2026-09-28 to 09-30, run on an earlier runtime without author isolation,
were used to pick tasks whose best first draft scored between 30% and
80% (place_phone_stand 31%, stack_bowls_two 77%, move_can_pot 73%, and
stack_bowls_three), with one deliberately harder task (hanging_mug) and
one deliberately easier task (place_burger_fries) added once each; on
2026-10-01 all formal campaigns were restarted on the isolated runtime
5.5.0, and place_dual_shoes was added after a further pilot on 10-06
(first drafts 82–84%). In the formal campaigns the first drafts of the
mid-difficulty tasks were already near the bar
([Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")),
higher than their pilots, which we report as observed; the pilot runtime
and the formal runtime differ in isolation and in the author’s host
account, and we do not attribute the difference to either. The second
experiment chose stack_bowls_three because it had never compiled.
Replication is unbalanced by design: tasks that did not compile were
repeated to see whether more budget helps (stack_bowls_three six times,
place_dual_shoes three), giving 20 campaigns with the primary author;
the no-feedback control was enabled on 10 of them, on four tasks, of
which 8 needed at least one repair round and therefore have a
comparison. Five further campaigns with a second author product
(hanging_mug, and two each of stack_bowls_three and place_dual_shoes)
test whether the pattern depends on the product. The pre-registered
second experiment
([Section 4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5 "Control lineages. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"))
ran three more campaigns on stack_bowls_three with 150 development seeds
and all three lineages, after the 20 primary campaigns and with their
outcomes known.

#### Authors and caller.

The primary author was Claude Code 2.1.284 running claude-opus-5-5 at
high effort, 2026-10-01 to 10-09; the second author was Codex CLI
0.160.0 running gpt-6-astra at high reasoning, 2026-10-07 to 10-10. Both
were used as shipped through their subscription channels, in a clean
per-campaign home directory linked only to their credentials, with
session environment variables removed and the locale fixed to English,
so that the tested object is the product and not the operator’s
configuration. Author cost is the API-equivalent amount the product
reports; the second product does not report one, and its cost is
recorded as unobservable rather than estimated. The Protocol B caller
was deepseek-flash (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on the provider’s price page),
accessed through its OpenAI-compatible API on 2026-10-09.

#### Budgets.

Per campaign: two R0 drafts, at most ten repair rounds, patience three,
a \$150 author-cost cap and a ten-hour author-time cap; development
target $`\geq 96\%`$ and validation target $`\geq 94\%`$ of usable
layouts; exam $`n{=}100`$ run to completion; caller check $`n{=}20`$.
Protocol B: 50 seeds per frozen skill, both arms on the same seeds.

#### What is reported.

For Q1: repair rounds, author cost and time, simulation episodes,
wall-clock, exam success and safety aborts with intervals, outcome, and
the RSI delta. For Q2: the write-once ablation, the per-round held-out
comparison, $`\mathrm{Learn}(k)`$, and what repair sessions read. For
Q3: per-arm success with intervals, safety aborts, decisions and invalid
decisions. For Q4: cost per episode and amortized cost. In addition: the
caller check, the isolation audit, speed, and the episode ledger as
data.

### 7.1 Q1: compiling to the qualification bar

[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
lists every campaign. 7 of 20 primary-author campaigns produced a
FrozenSkill, on 4 of 7 tasks; 4 reached the R1 targets and failed the
exam, and 9 ended R1 on a budget rule. The seven frozen skills cost
\$4.29–8.22 of author budget (median \$6.69), 1.4–2.9 author-hours in
2–4 sessions, and 5.2–13.0 wall-clock hours including every simulated
episode. Five of the seven needed no repair round: the better of two
first drafts met the development and validation targets, and the exam
confirmed it. The two others needed one and two rounds. Campaigns that
did not compile cost \$10.97–48.28 (median \$36.74), with
stack_bowls_three alone consuming \$202 over six campaigns; across all
20 campaigns the author bill was \$384 for 78 session-hours, and
campaigns ran 262–1177 simulated episodes (median 532). No campaign
failed the speed or regression rule: exam versions ran at 1.18$`\times`$
the expert’s median simulated time (at most 1.49$`\times`$ against a
limit of $`2\times`$).

Exam success itself was high: 12 of 20 campaigns scored at least 95,
including every campaign on five of the seven tasks; the eight below 95
are five of the six three-object-stack campaigns (78, 90, 86, 90, 89, 95
over the six) and the three bimanual shoe campaigns (78, 90, 88). What
separated passing from failing among the twelve was the safety rule, to
which we return next. The RSI delta, exam minus validation baseline, is
near zero for zero-repair campaigns, as it must be (the same version
measured on two layout sets); on the 14 campaigns with at least one
repair round it averaged +13.3 points (median +9.9; range -5.3 to +39.4;
positive in 12 of 14), with the largest gains (+39.4, +34.4, +28.5,
+22.3) on the lowest starting points. Baseline and delta are strongly
anticorrelated ($`r=-0.88`$), partly by construction; the more telling
statistic is the exam itself: repaired campaigns that started below 80%
on validation averaged 88.9 on the exam and those that started at or
above 80% averaged 92.1. The baseline and the exam are nearly
uncorrelated on the repaired campaigns ($`r=0.10`$): repair lifts
different starting points to a ceiling that is set mostly by the task
([Figure 2](#S7.F2 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")b).

The pre-registered second experiment
([Table 3](#S7.T3 "In 7.1 Q1: compiling to the qualification bar ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"))
repeated stack_bowls_three three times with 128 usable development
layouts instead of 43. Its primary outcome is 0 frozen of 3: the repair
lineages reached 120/128, 122/128 and 122/128 on development, one to
three layouts short of the 96% target, ended on the patience rule after
4, 6, 8 rounds, and scored 88, 93, 94 on the exam with 8, 5, 3 safety
aborts. With the six earlier campaigns the task is 0 of 9 frozen at
78–95 success and 3–16 aborts per 100. The RSI deltas were +1.3, +26.3,
+20.7 points, so two of the three campaigns moved a low starting point
most of the way to the ceiling; the task’s ceiling, not the author’s
progress toward it, is what stays below the gate. Each campaign cost
\$61.2–119.7 of author budget across its three lineages (\$104 repair,
\$78 control and \$96 inherit-only in total) and 47–74 wall-clock hours.

### 7.2 The gate binds on rare safety aborts, not on task completion

Twelve primary-author campaigns scored at least 95 and seven passed; the
five that did not were stopped by the safety rule alone, with 1, 1, 3,
2, 4 aborts in 100 episodes at success rates of 95–97. Of the eight
campaigns below 95, the five three-object-stack campaigns also aborted
often (4–16 per 100) and the three shoe campaigns rarely (0–1). Every
one of the 75 exam aborts across the 25 campaigns was a physical
envelope violation: 61 were objects pushed out of the workspace box and
14 were objects dropped below the table plane; no exam episode was
stopped for an invalid pose request or a joint limit. A 100-episode exam
is a coarse instrument for events at this rate: zero aborts in 100
bounds the per-episode abort probability only to 3.6% (Clopper–Pearson
95%), one abort to 5.4%, and a skill whose true abort rate is 1% passes
a zero-abort rule with probability 37% (2%: 13%; 3%: 5%). Two
place_phone_stand campaigns illustrate the consequence: the first passed
with 0/100 and the third failed with 1/100, and their abort-rate
intervals overlap almost entirely.

To see whether the failures were sampling luck, the exam versions of the
four campaigns nearest the bar were re-run on 300 further layouts
([Table 4](#S7.T4 "In 7.2 The gate binds on rare safety aborts, not on task completion ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds");
report-only). All four scored 96–97% success, but their abort rates
separated into three tiers: essentially zero, about 1%, and 3–4%. The
exam had scored them 1, 1, 4 and 2 aborts, in that order. The two
stack_bowls_two verdicts were therefore correct, the place_phone_stand
verdict was probably unlucky, and hanging_mug sits where a binary
zero-abort rule cannot decide. Repair did not remove these tail events:
campaigns with large RSI deltas still aborted in the exam (hanging_mug
reached 42/42 development and 43/43 validation and aborted once in 100;
stack_bowls_two 3 reached 47/47 and aborted four times), which is
expected, since development and validation blocks of 36–47 layouts
cannot reveal a 1–3% event often enough for the author to act on it. For
each of the 7 frozen skills, its 100 exam episodes and its caller-check
episodes contain no abort, which bounds that skill’s abort rate only to
about 3.0%; the skill that later aborted in reuse
([Section 7.6](#S7.SS6 "7.6 Q3: reuse by executors that did not author the skill ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"))
sits inside that bound. The second experiment tested the obvious remedy:
with 128 usable development layouts a 3% abort rate appears about four
times per version, yet the three campaigns still aborted 8, 5, 3 times
in their exams (13 workspace exits, 3 drops). More layouts moved the
exam scores to the top of the task’s range but did not clear the gate.
The aborts were not hidden from the author this time: the versions that
went to the exam had aborted 7, 4, 4 times on the 128 development
layouts (exam: 8, 5, 3), every repair-round version aborted at least 4
times there, and the starting versions had aborted 6, 36, 16 times. The
author read these aborts in its feedback each round, reduced them from
36 to 4 per 128 in one campaign, and never removed them.

| Campaign      | Exam | Aborts | Success /300 | 95% CI    | Aborts | 95% CI  |
|---------------|------|--------|--------------|-----------|--------|---------|
| phone_stand 3 | 95   | 1      | 290/300      | 94.0–98.2 | 0      | 0.0–1.2 |
| hanging_mug 1 | 97   | 1      | 290/300      | 94.0–98.2 | 3      | 0.2–2.9 |
| bowls_two 3   | 96   | 4      | 288/300      | 93.1–97.7 | 8      | 1.2–5.2 |
| bowls_two 2   | 95   | 2      | 288/300      | 93.1–97.7 | 11     | 1.8–6.5 |

### 7.3 Q2a: in-session self-testing shows no detectable effect

Every first draft in
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
was written in a session in which the author could run practice episodes
and its own simulator experiments.
[Table 5](#S7.T5 "In 7.3 Q2a: in-session self-testing shows no detectable effect ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
compares the validation baselines of those drafts with drafts written
under the two ablation conditions on the same scene (write once on all
six tasks, practice only on four). Removing the simulator account
(practice only) and removing practice altogether (write once) changed
neither the first-draft development scores nor the validation baselines
detectably: the task-stratified difference between the default condition
and write-once is -3.4 points on the validation baseline (permutation
$`p=0.77`$, one-sided for the default being better) and +0.5 points on
development scores ($`p=0.48`$); practice-only versus write-once is -3.9
($`p=0.97`$). Write-once drafts reached 76–98% on validation from the
task card, the official environment source and the API alone. Very poor
drafts occurred with and without the ability to run the package
(move_can_pot 13/45 and stack_bowls_three 11/43 with full practice;
hanging_mug 6/42 write-once), and the two-draft selection absorbed them
in each case. With one write-once campaign per task, this is evidence of
no detectable effect rather than of none: the within-task spread of
default baselines (SD 11.8 points over 13 degrees of freedom) gives the
stratified difference a standard error of about 5.7 points, so a
one-sided test at 80% power would detect only a difference of about 14
points or more. Within that limit, the in-session term of the
decomposition in
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not ‣ 3 Setting and Terminology ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
is small for this author, and the measurable self-improvement in a
campaign is the cross-session term.

| Task        | Default  | Practice only | Write once |
|-------------|----------|---------------|------------|
| phone_stand | 88.3 (3) | 85.0 (2)      | 92.5 (1)   |
| bowls_two   | 95.9 (3) | 96.3 (2)      | 97.6 (1)   |
| can_pot     | 95.5 (3) | 96.6 (2)      | 95.5 (1)   |
| hanging_mug | 83.7 (1) | 75.6 (2)      | 83.7 (1)   |
| dual_shoes  | 76.9 (3) | –             | 86.1 (1)   |
| bowls_three | 70.4 (6) | –             | 75.6 (1)   |

### 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance

[Table 6](#S7.T6 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
and
[Figure 2](#S7.F2 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")a
give the per-round comparison on the 8 controlled campaigns that needed
repair. Each repair version $`R1.k`$ and each control draft $`C.k`$,
written in sessions of the same length limit from the same inputs except
for history and evidence, was run once on the same hidden validation
layouts (36–45 per task; about 3,200 episodes in all). Repair was better
in 26 of 34 rounds, worse in 7 and tied in 1, by +6.4 layouts (+15.0
points) per round on average; per campaign the mean difference was
positive in 8 of 8 (one-sided sign test $`p=0.004`$; exact sign-flip
permutation on campaign means +5.7 layouts, $`p=0.004`$). The same
comparison on the development layouts, where the repair side has an
advantage, gives 29 of 34 rounds better (+6.2 layouts), so the advantage
is not an artifact of tuning to the development block.

Two further readings guard against the asymmetry noted in
[Section 4](#S4.SS0.SSS0.Px5 "Control lineages. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds").
Relative to each campaign’s own starting point on the same hidden
layouts, the repair lineage averaged above the start in 8 of 8 campaigns
(mean +4.3 layouts; sign test $`p=0.004`$), while the control drafts
averaged below it in 6 of 8 (mean -1.3), which is what a single draw
against a selected best-of-two predicts; part of the per-round gap is
therefore the starting point that repair keeps and a rewrite forfeits.
The selection-matched best-of-$`k`$ comparison of
[Equation 1](#S4.E1 "In Control lineages. ‣ 4 Protocol A: Compiling a Skill ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
is much closer: on the development layouts, $`\mathrm{Learn}(k)`$ at the
end of R1 was -2, +2, +1, +2, +0, +0, +7, +2 layouts (positive in 5
campaigns, zero in 2, negative in 1), and on the hidden layouts each
side’s best version favors repair in 5 campaigns and the control in 3.
Independent rewrites have enormous variance, from 4/45 to 44/45 within
one campaign, so a handful of them occasionally contain a version as
good as the repair lineage’s best. What repair buys is not a higher
ceiling than lucky rewriting but reliability per round.

The second experiment separates the two things a repair session has that
a rewrite does not
([Table 7](#S7.T7 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"),
[Figure 3](#S7.F3 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
On the 45 hidden layouts, repair exceeded the from-scratch rewrite by
+10.2 layouts per round on average (per campaign +15.8, +6.3, +8.5); the
inherit-only lineage, which revises the previous version with its own
practice runs but without the runtime’s development-layout feedback,
exceeded the rewrite by +8.7 (+12.5, +5.3, +8.4); and repair exceeded
inherit-only by +1.5 (+3.2, +1.0, +0.1). All three differences had the
same sign in all 3 campaigns, which with three campaigns as the unit is
the smallest attainable one-sided sign-test $`p`$ of 0.125; the
per-round counts (16/1/1, 14/3/1 and 11/6/1 better/worse/tied for the
three differences) are descriptive, since rounds within a lineage are
not independent, and none of these results is claimed as significant.
Within those limits the answer to Q2 is: on layouts none of the lineages
has seen, revising the previous version beats rewriting from scratch,
most of the gap comes from inheriting the previous version across
sessions, and the runtime’s development-layout feedback adds a little
more at the margin. Both are components of self-improvement in the sense
of
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not ‣ 3 Setting and Terminology ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds");
neither is selection, which all three lineages share. The mechanism is
consistent with this reading: of the 60 repair sessions of the primary
author, 60 read the per-layout feedback of the previous version, 59 read
the comparison verdict, 60 read the author’s own notes, and 56 (93%)
cite specific failure classes, scores or layout seeds in the delivered
rationale; the development feedback is read and used, and its marginal
value over inheritance and the author’s own practice on this task is
small. The remaining gap between repair and the gate is the one
described in
[Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 The gate binds on rare safety aborts, not on task completion ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"):
on the hard tasks, repair drove development scores to within a few
layouts of the target and validation to about 90%, and the exam then
found aborts that the development block showed too rarely to act on.

### 7.5 A second author product

The five campaigns with Codex CLI 0.160.0
([Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"),
lower block) reproduce the pattern without a control group. First drafts
started at 80–98% on validation, 1–7 repair rounds moved development
scores to 38–43 of 42–44, and the exams scored 83–96 with 1, 1, 0, 9, 5
aborts (in the order of
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"));
1 of five reached the success bar and none passed the gate: four aborted
at least once and the fifth scored 93, for the same two reasons as the
primary author on the same tasks (success of 83 on the three-object
stack and 93–94 on the shoe task; a single abort on hanging_mug at 96).
RSI deltas were small (-1.7 to +3.0) because the starting points were
high. The product’s subscription quota ran out twice; the runtime paused
and resumed the session’s remaining time without counting a round. All
five audits were clean. These campaigns show that the protocol transfers
to another agent product; they are not a comparison of the two products’
strength, which would need matched tasks and budgets.

at all the skills succeeded in 148/150 episodes (98.7%; Wilson

### 7.7 Q4: cost per episode

Compiling the three skills cost \$20.20 of author budget in total
(\$5.46–7.99 each). That is the cost of the campaigns that succeeded;
the program that produced the seven frozen skills cost \$384 over 20
campaigns, or \$55 per frozen skill and \$96 per compiled task, and the
second experiment added \$278 for three campaigns that did not compile.
Simulation is not priced: the 25 compile campaigns occupied 366
simulator-slot hours on one GPU
([Section 7.8](#S7.SS8 "7.8 Caller check, audit, and the episode ledger ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")),
which at a rental price of one to two dollars per GPU-hour would add an
amount comparable to the author bill; the runtime’s own engineering is a
fixed cost we do not amortize. Executing a frozen skill has no model
cost per episode with code and \$0.00028–0.00054 with the caller; the
150 caller episodes cost \$0.055 together. With compilation amortized
([Figure 4](#S7.F4 "In 7.7 Q4: cost per episode ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")b),
the per-episode cost of the most expensive skill with the caller is
\$0.080 at 100 deployments and \$0.0083 at 1000, below one cent. We do
not report a break-even against direct online control, because the
direct-control arms of the full design were not run as a formal
evaluation. The only evidence is a runtime self-test of two episodes per
arm on move_can_pot with the same prompt template and a package that
exposes only the primitives: the primary author’s model, controlling the
robot directly, succeeded in 0 of 2 episodes at \$4.77 per episode and
9.5 decisions (about 201k output tokens per episode), and DeepSeek-flash
in 0 of 2 at \$0.039. These four episodes fix an order of magnitude, not
a rate: per-episode reasoning from primitives costs dollars with the
strong model and cents with the cheap one, and in this sample completed
nothing; a compiled skill costs a fraction of a cent and completes 98%.
The order of magnitude agrees with the one public figure we know of for
per-episode reasoning with evolved experience: EmbodiedEvo reports a
mean model-API cost of \$5.73 per test episode for a GPT-6 Astra agent
carrying its Skills and Lessons, excluding the playground learning
phase \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. That figure comes from different tasks, a
different simulator and a different observation interface, is not a
measurement of ours, and does not enter any break-even computation; it
only says that the per-episode cost of the route we compare against is
dollars, not cents.

### 7.8 Caller check, audit, and the episode ledger

The post-freeze caller check with the author product scored 137 of 138
valid episodes over the seven frozen skills (99.3%; two of the 140
scheduled episodes failed on infrastructure in every attempt), with
1.0–3.1 decisions per episode; no skill approached the warning
threshold. The isolation audit graded 17 of 20 primary-author campaigns
clean, 2 metadata and 1 review; the three non-clean grades record that
another campaign’s identifier or home path appeared in a process or
directory listing, with no file content read. Process listings are
visible across users on both machines; this is a known gap of the
isolation, not a contamination, and the three campaigns are retained.
The second author’s five audits were clean. In the second experiment two
campaigns were clean and one (j2) was graded review for the same reason,
another campaign’s directory name and identifiers in a process listing
with no content read; it was reviewed and retained, and removing it does
not change the sign of any of the three differences in
[Table 8](#S7.T8 "In 7.4 Q2b: repair beats rewriting on hidden layouts, and most of the gap is inheritance ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds").

Every episode of both protocols is in the hash-chained ledger with its
seed, version, mode, outcome, failure class, safety events, primitive
calls, simulated and wall-clock time, and the entry and exit marks of
each atom call, so that the primitive trajectory is segmented by
sub-goal and labelled with the atom’s name and its ok value. The 25
compile campaigns alone recorded 18,941 episodes (14,466 in the protocol
itself, of which 2,938 were the author’s practice runs, and 4,475 in the
report-only re-runs); 177 (0.9%) were infrastructure failures and are
excluded, leaving 18,764 labelled trajectories, 15,909 successful and
2,855 failed with a cause (1,684 finished without satisfying the
predicate, 893 workspace exits, 254 drops, 21 atom errors, 2 invalid
pose requests, 1 budget exhaustion). Every fallback episode is
segmented: a trajectory contains 8.4 atom calls and 5.6 top-level
sub-goals on average (5.3 in failed episodes), 99.2% of fallback
episodes have every primitive call inside an atom, and none bypasses the
atoms. A valid trajectory took a median 70 s of simulator-slot time, so
the study produced 51.3 labelled trajectories per slot-hour (366
slot-hours in all) and 60.5 per campaign wall-clock hour with four
slots. These traces carry sub-goal boundaries, language (from SKILL.md),
success labels and failure types, which teleoperation data lack, but not
control-frequency sensor streams; their value as training data for
embodied models is not tested here
([Section 8](#S8 "8 Discussion ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).
````
