### 7.9 Published results on the same tasks, for reference

[Table 10](#S7.T10 "In 7.8 Caller check, audit, and the episode ledger ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
places the exam results beside the numbers that the RoboTwin 2.0 paper
reports on the same seven tasks, simulator and
embodiment \[[65](#bib.bib65)\]: five policies trained from 50 clean
demonstrations per task (its Table 10, Easy and Hard settings; version
v2 of arXiv:2506.18088), its own LLM-generated task programs (its
Table 9), and the official expert program (its Table 11). All five
policies and all seven tasks are listed. None of these numbers were
measured here, and the conditions differ in data, run-time information,
scene and metric, as the caption lists; the table is context, not a
comparison, and we compute no differences and draw no ranking from it.
Three directional observations are all we take from it. First, the seven
tasks are not easy for demonstration-trained policies: 24 of the 35 Easy
entries are below 60% and 32 of the 35 Hard entries are below 25%.
Second, the LLM-generated code of RoboTwin 2.0, which reads privileged
object poses, scores 0 on place_phone_stand and hanging_mug. Third, the
skills compiled here, with no demonstrations and no privileged poses,
scored 78–100 of 100 on exams drawn after freezing in a scene tier that
lies between Easy and Hard, at \$4.29–8.22 of author spend per frozen
skill (\$55 at program level,
[Section 7.7](#S7.SS7 "7.7 Q4: cost per episode ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")),
where the demonstration route spends 50 demonstrations and a fine-tuning
run per task; the two cost accountings are not convertible into each
other. The one entry measured under our own conditions is the official
expert program in phase 0: on stack_bowls_three it succeeded in 4–6 of
10 episodes across 12 campaigns, while the compiled skills for that task
scored 78–95 on the exam and were stopped by the safety rule, not by
task completion
([Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 The gate binds on rare safety aborts, not on task completion ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")).

## 8 Discussion

#### Skills before scale.

The results test the precondition of the hypothesis stated in the
introduction, not the hypothesis. A strong general model compiled four
of seven tasks into skills that passed a qualification exam on layouts
drawn after freezing, for under ten dollars each; the skills ran on new
layouts without that model at the same success, and a model from another
family could drive them from the description alone for a fraction of a
cent per episode. What the experiments do not show is that skill
execution data improve an embodied model, nor that any of this transfers
to physical hardware. If both hold, the order of the language-model
history can be inverted for robots: the strong general model exists now,
skills compiled from it can put robots to work in bounded scenes now,
and the labelled trajectories that execution produces are the corpus
that embodied foundation models lack. If either fails, compiled skills
remain a deployment technique with a measured cost profile.

#### What recursion bought, and what it did not.

Five of the seven frozen skills needed no repair: on the easy tasks the
first draft was already at the bar, and the protocol’s contribution was
qualification and freezing, not improvement. Recursion mattered on the
other tasks, and there its effect is characterized by the controls: on
layouts none of the lineages has seen, a session that revises the
previous version delivers a better version than a session that starts
over, in 8 of 8 and 3 of 3 campaigns, and the inherit-only lineage shows
that most of that advantage is carried by the artifact itself, by
inheriting the previous version across sessions, with the runtime’s
development feedback adding a smaller increment on the task where we
measured it. Both are self-improvement of the skill in the sense of
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What we call RSI, and what we do not ‣ 3 Setting and Terminology ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds");
the finding says where in the loop the improvement lives. What recursion
did not do is carry a hard task over the gate: stack_bowls_three failed
on safety aborts in all 9 campaigns, with 43 and with 128 usable
development layouts, even as the RSI delta reached +39.4 points. The
larger block let the author see the aborts (7, 4, 4 on 128 development
layouts for the versions it sent to the exam, at least 4 for every
repair-round version) and did not let it remove them, so the hypothesis
that the loop merely lacked evidence is not supported by this
experiment; the bottleneck is now more plausibly the strategies the
author finds for this task and the kernel they run on than the amount of
feedback. One hypothesis, not a result, follows from the kernel’s
design: the planner does not see the objects on the table
([Section 6](#S6 "6 Experimental Setup ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")),
and the dominant abort is an object pushed out of the workspace (61 of
75 exam aborts across the 25 campaigns of both products, 13 of 16 in the
second experiment), which is what an arm sweeping through a third bowl
or a distractor would produce; a planner that treats detected objects as
obstacles would test it. Abort-focused evidence between rounds, which we
proposed after the first results, remains untested and is no longer the
obvious next step.

#### Gates for rare events.

A zero-abort rule over 100 episodes is a coin flip for skills whose true
abort rate is near 1%, and it passes a 3% skill one time in twenty. The
300-layout re-evaluations separated tiers that the exam could not. A
better gate would state the safety requirement as an upper confidence
bound on the abort rate, or as a sequential test that stops early on
clearly safe or clearly unsafe skills \[[72](#bib.bib72)\]; both cost
more simulation than 100 episodes and both cost nothing in model calls,
since the exam runs in fallback mode. Reporting the interval beside the
verdict, as
[Table 2](#S7.T2 "In 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
does, is the minimum. As a post-hoc observation, not a change to the
pre-registered rule: under a success-only rule 12 of 20 primary
campaigns and 1 of five GPT-6 campaigns would have passed, and under a
rule that bounds the abort rate by its upper confidence limit no
campaign with an observed abort would, so the gate’s verdicts are
sensitive to how the safety requirement is written.

#### What is externalized.

The executor crossings answer a question that success rates alone
cannot: where the capability lives. If only the author’s model could
execute the skill, the package would be a reasoning scaffold and the
capability would still be in the runtime. Here an executor with no model
matches the author’s exam, and a cheap caller from another family adds
nothing on these tasks and loses nothing, because the descriptions
rarely need interpretation: one plan per episode, or one recovery
branch. The kernel keeps motion generation, collision checking and
limits; the skill holds decomposition, sub-goal ordering, preconditions,
postconditions, observation timing, bounded recoveries and permissions;
the caller, when present, holds branch selection. Tasks whose recovery
sections are long or ambiguous would load the caller more, and the gap
between callers would then measure the description; we did not observe
such a task among the three measured. EmbodiedEvo’s finding that
experience evolved with a strong model raises the success of two weaker
models that read it \[[14](#bib.bib14)\] points in the same direction as
our cross-family caller, with the difference that the weaker models
there still reason in every episode, whereas here the description is
enough for a caller to execute a package it never saw the code of.

#### Strategy substitution versus perception completion.

Text corpora do not contain grip forces, and the author has no tactile
input, yet skills for fragile or slippery objects can be compiled if the
author discovers a strategy whose success does not depend on the missing
quantity: supporting an object from below instead of pinching it, or
re-grasping after a slip check, rather than estimating a safe force. Our
tasks contain no such hidden property, so this is a hypothesis grounded
in the mechanism rather than a result; RoboTwin 2.0 has no fragile or
low-friction assets, and adding them would change the official code tree
that the tamper check pins. The boundary is also clear: tasks that
require identifying the property, such as sorting real from artificial
eggs, cannot be solved by substitution, and there the
modality-completion route \[[60](#bib.bib60), [59](#bib.bib59)\] is the
only one.

#### When is an author worth paying for.

The author is expensive per session and the executor is nearly free per
episode, so the economics depend on reuse and on failure. The seven
frozen skills cost under \$10 each; the nine primary campaigns that did
not compile cost \$10.97–48.28 each and the three of the second
experiment \$61.2–119.7, and all returned a ledger and a near-miss
package, not a skill, so the cost of a program of compilation is
dominated by the tasks that fail: \$55 per frozen skill in this program
against \$6.69 for the median successful campaign. A task that a strong
model solves at 95% on the first draft needs only qualification and
freezing; a task that it solves at 60% needs repair and may still fail
the safety rule. The break-even question against per-episode reasoning
remains open for lack of a measured direct-control baseline; the
self-test suggests the answer is a small number of deployments.

#### Threats to validity.

The author may have seen RoboTwin 2.0 during pretraining; exam and reuse
layouts are drawn after freezing, so memorization of public content
cannot supply exam answers, but it can make first drafts stronger than
they would be on a private task suite, and the write-once result should
be read with that in mind. The task card includes the success-predicate
source, so the author writes against the criterion; we consider that the
realistic setting for a scene an integrator specifies, but it is a
lenient one. The held-out comparison and the 300-layout re-evaluations
were added after the first results were seen and are reported as such.
Replication is unbalanced and small: one to six campaigns per task,
eight controlled campaigns, three skills in Protocol B with one cheap
caller; intervals carry that uncertainty, and cross-task summaries are
medians, not pooled rates. DeepSeek prices vary by time of day and the
price snapshot is dated. Process listings were visible across isolated
users. The author products are closed subscription services: their
served models, system prompts and tools can change behind a fixed
version string and cannot be archived, so Protocol A outcomes are a
dated measurement of two products rather than of a method that a reader
can re-run, and only the Protocol B episodes are replayable from stored
responses. The second experiment deviated from its registration in
execution (voided rounds after a provider login failure, a redrawn exam,
operator restarts after connection drops;
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Pre-registration of the Second Experiment and Deviation Record ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds"));
none of the deviations changed a rule or a result after it was seen.
Finally, the runtime version advanced during the study; the increments
are listed with their dates and none touched the author prompt or a gate
rule.

## 9 Limitations and Safety

The study is simulation-only; friction, compliance, calibration drift
and human proximity produce failures a clean simulator does not, and no
real-robot run is reported, whereas EmbodiedRSI reports real-robot
results \[[15](#bib.bib15)\]. Seven tasks on one scene tier is a small
suite next to the 42 RoboDojo tasks of concurrent
work \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. Our author receives RGB-D images and camera
calibration and writes its own perception, while EmbodiedEvo’s agent
works from RGB alone, so the two settings are not directly comparable in
perception difficulty. Restricted Python trades expressiveness for
verifiability and cannot express contact-rich dexterity. The primitive
API has single-arm actions, so bimanual coordination is serialized.
Passing an exam is empirical evidence about declared layouts, harness
versions and safety envelopes, not a proof of physical safety; the
exam’s resolution for rare events is stated in
[Section 7.2](#S7.SS2 "7.2 The gate binds on rare safety aborts, not on task completion ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds").
Tamper evidence detects changes; it does not prevent deliberate forgery,
and session transcripts are retained for audit. The author reads the
success predicate. Protocol B ran its minimal form: no second or third
caller family, no strong-model caller, no format smoke test, and no
formal direct-control baseline, so non-inferiority margins and
break-even counts from the full design are not reported. The
inherit-only comparison rests on three campaigns of one task with one
author product and is existence evidence; the inherit-only author still
receives one bit of information per round (whether the head was
replaced), keeps its own practice runs, and works from a fresh host
account, and the two changes of the second experiment were introduced
together. Process listings are visible across the isolated users on both
machines, so another campaign’s identifiers can be seen, though not its
content. Meta-level improvement of the author’s procedure is not
claimed. Physical deployment requires isolation during testing,
emergency stops, force and speed limits, independent monitoring and
staged release, none of which the protocols supply.

## 10 Conclusion

We separated the authoring of robot skills from their execution and
measured the separation. A strong general model, used only offline,
produced 7 immutable skill packages on 4 of 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks that
passed a qualification exam on layouts drawn after freezing, most of
them from a first draft that needed only qualification, at \$4.29–8.22
each and \$55 per skill when the failed campaigns are counted. The three
tasks that did not compile were stopped by rare safety aborts that a
100-episode exam can barely resolve and that a larger development block
did not remove. On hidden layouts, revising the previous version beat
rewriting from scratch in every controlled campaign, and an inherit-only
lineage located most of that advantage in the inherited artifact rather
than in the feedback read about it; self-testing within a session showed
no detectable effect on first drafts. A second author product behaved
the same way. The frozen skills ran at 98.7% on new layouts with no
model and at 98.0% with a caller from another family at a fraction of a
cent of model cost per episode. The protocols, ledgers and seeds are
released so that the same measurements can be repeated with other
authors, executors and tasks. Whether the data these skills produce
while working can, in turn, train the embodied models that do not yet
exist is the question the next study should ask.

## Data and Code Availability

The compile and reuse runtimes, adapters, task configurations, prompts,
seed generators, environment fingerprints, hash-chained ledgers, raw
caller responses, analysis scripts and the frozen skill packages are
released at
[https://github.com/Orillusion/embodied-skill-rsi](https://github.com/Orillusion/embodied-skill-rsi)
(release v1.0): the code under Apache-2.0, the data, ledgers and frozen
skills under CC BY 4.0. The released runtime is the 5.9.0 release build;
it differs from the frozen build used in the experiments only in site
configuration (docs/runtime_release_vs_frozen_5.9.0.diff). Author
session transcripts, raw model inputs and outputs, and per-episode
images are not released and are retained for audit. python3
analysis/reproduce.py rebuilds the main tables from the public ledgers
and checks them automatically; it needs no GPU. Third-party assets and
model weights remain under their original licenses.

## Ethics Statement

The experiments use simulated robots and commercial model products
accessed through their ordinary subscription or API channels; no human
participants, personal data or animals are involved. Any physical
deployment of compiled skills requires institutional safety review.

## Generative AI Use

Generative AI systems were used to support literature organization,
language drafting, figure scaffolding and protocol structuring, and, as
the object of study, to author skills. The runtime, the analysis scripts
and the released repository were written and tested with the assistance
of a generative AI coding product (Claude Code) and were reviewed and
verified by the authors. All technical claims, citations, methods,
analyses, code and final text were verified and approved by the human
authors, who retain full responsibility.

| Primitive | Signature | Returns | Cost |
|----|----|----|----|

| observe | () | ok, one component per role, table-height estimate | 1 |

| gripper_state | (arm) | commanded, measured, open | 0 |

| wait | (seconds $`\leq 2`$) | bool | 1 |

against the 90-call episode budget. Every move_pose and gripper call is
an independent planning request; the official plan-success latch is
reset before each call.

Restricted-Python rules for skills.py and perception.py: no import; no
while, try, class or lambda; a builtin allowlist (arithmetic, len,
range, min, max, abs, sorted, enumerate, zip, list and dict literals);
no names beginning with an underscore; a static source-line limit. The
validator is the same file for every author and every executor.

## Appendix B Gate Parameters and Qualification Checklist

|  Parameter |  Value |  Rationale |
|----|----|----|
|  Scene tier |  clutter (demo_clean + up to 10 distractors; fixed lighting; no table-height randomization) |  the fully randomized tier was too easy in a pilot (first drafts above 82%); table-height randomization conflicts with absolute-height success predicates |
|  R0 drafts |  2 |  independent starting points differ more than one lineage’s repairs |
|  Development layouts |  50 seeds (70000–70049); 42–47 usable |  separates 85% from 95% versions; layouts the generator cannot stabilize are dropped for every version |
|  Validation layouts |  50 seeds (71000–71049); 36–46 usable |  hidden; used for the baseline, the target check and the held-out re-run; never fed back |
|  Development / validation target |  $`\geq 96\%`$ / $`\geq 94\%`$ of usable |  first integers at or above 95% on 50, one layout of slack against a hidden set |
|  Max repair rounds / patience |  10 / 3 |  budget bound; three consecutive non-improvements ends R1 |
|  Author cost / time cap |  \$150 / 10 h |  per campaign; exhaustion is reported as not compiled |
|  Author session limit |  1 h |  pilot sessions before the limit took 31–111 min; background work does not survive a session |
|  Practice |  $`\leq 30`$ episodes per round; own simulator account |  the author’s means of in-session testing; logged |
|  Exam |  $`n{=}100`$, seeds from $`[10^{5},10^{6})`$ drawn after freezing |  point-estimate threshold; interval half-width about 4.5 points at the threshold; the interval is reported beside every verdict |
|  Exam decision / completion |  fail at $`>5`$ failures; always run to completion; one attempt |  keeps failed campaigns comparable; no retake |
|  Safety / speed / regression |  0 aborts; $`\leq 2\times`$ expert median; not worse than any accepted head |  a slow or regressed skill is not reusable |
|  Settle before judging |  2 simulated s |  an object released at the last moment is judged at rest |
|  Caller check |  20 episodes, author product, 4 decisions $`\times`$ 8 steps |  report only; warning if $`>15`$ points below exam |
|  Re-evaluation (5.5.3) |  300 new layouts, exam version |  report only; resolves abort rates the exam cannot |
|  Held-out re-run (5.8.0) |  every $`R1.k`$ and $`C.k`$ on the validation layouts |  report only; the per-round comparison on unseen layouts |
|  Second experiment (5.9.0, pre-registered 2026-10-10) |  150 development seeds (128 usable); inherit-only lineage $`I.k`$ (practice runs kept, no development-layout feedback), rounds matched to repair, own host account, not examined; gate, targets and limits unchanged |  tests whether a block that shows 1–3% aborts lets repair clear the gate, and separates inheritance from the development feedback |
|  Protocol B seeds |  50 per skill, exam range, excluding all manifest seeds |  disjoint from every compile-time seed |
|  Protocol B caller |  deepseek-flash, temperature 0, 32,768 output tokens, 12 decisions, 900 s per decision |  temperature 0 (hosted decoding is not bit-reproducible); the decision cap is reported as a mean, not reached |

Table 12: Parameters of Protocol A and Protocol B as run. All Protocol A
values were fixed before the first campaign; the two report-only
evaluations were added during the study at the versions shown.

Before release each package must satisfy: (1) the front matter validates
and atoms matches ATOMS; (2) both Python files pass the
restricted-Python validator; (3) every atom returns a dictionary with
ok; (4) fallback(api) completes without an uncaught error on every
development layout; (5) development and validation targets are met;
(6) the ledger chain, runtime manifest and official tree verify;
(7) exam, safety, speed and regression gates pass; (8) files are hashed,
the manifest is written, and the bundle is copied to the frozen store.

## Appendix C Prompts

The author prompt (TASK.md, about 12 KB, identical for both products and
every campaign) states the task, the four deliverables, the two run
modes, the judging rule (fallback exam at $`\geq 95\%`$ on unseen
layouts with zero safety aborts, speed and regression), the primitive
API and its semantics, the per-episode limits and the settle period, the
rules of the test (API-only access at run time; no modification of
evaluator, runtime or ledgers; no external interpretation of results;
only the author’s own working directory and host account), the practice
tool and, in the default condition, the host account. Each repair round
adds a short note naming the round and the practice budget and pointing
to the history directory with every earlier version, its feedback and
its verdict. The caller prompt states the caller’s role, the plan format
(one to eight steps of atom call, observe or state), the decision limit,
the shared call budget, the instruction to follow the standard flow and,
on failure, the recovery section of SKILL.md, and the JSON answer
format; it is identical for the caller check and for Protocol B. In the
write-once condition the practice paragraphs are replaced by one
sentence stating that no simulator is available and the package cannot
be run before delivery. Full prompt texts are released with the code.

## Appendix E Pre-registration of the Second Experiment and Deviation Record

The following is a condensed translation of the registration written
into the protocol on 2026-10-10, before any campaign of the second
experiment ran, and of the deviation record appended during execution;
the original text is released with the code.

#### Registered design.

Task stack_bowls_three, clutter tier, Claude Code as author, three
campaigns. Development seeds 70000–70149 (150; the validation block
71000–71049 unchanged for comparability). Three lineages from the same
R0 starting point with the same product, practice budget and 60-minute
sessions: repair (unchanged), no-feedback rewrite (unchanged), and
inherit-only, which copies the starting workspace with the author’s
notes and practice records, deletes the starting version’s feedback and
verdict, revises the previous version each round with the same practice
budget, and receives none of the runtime’s development-layout results
for any version (no development evidence in the workspace or the host
view; the task card and round prompt say so); the runtime keeps the best
inherit-only version by the same strict-improvement rule and reports
only HEAD. Rounds matched to repair, run in the background; own host
account; not charged to the repair cost and time caps; not examined.
Gate, ladder (ten rounds, patience three, 96% and 94% targets) and exam
(100 episodes, $`\geq 95\%`$ and zero aborts) unchanged. Primary
outcome: campaigns frozen out of three, descriptive. Secondary outcomes:
RSI delta and exam aborts per campaign beside the six earlier campaigns;
after each campaign, the starting version and every repair, control and
inherit-only version run once on the hidden validation layouts, paired
by round as repair$`-`$inherit, inherit$`-`$control and
repair$`-`$control, with a one-sided sign test over campaigns and
descriptive per-round counts; development-layout curves descriptive
only. Registered limitations: the larger block and the new lineage are
introduced together; the inherit-only author still learns whether HEAD
changed; its host account is new; three campaigns on one task are
existence evidence.

#### Deviations recorded during execution.

- •
  2026-10-11: the first three campaigns (i1–i3) were voided before any
  author session because the queue did not pass the new flags; they
  stopped in phase 0 and were re-queued unchanged as j1–j3.
- •
  2026-10-12 and 10-13/14: the SSH relay to the simulation host dropped
  several times; the coordinator was restarted each time with no author
  session in progress, existing episode results were kept and unfinished
  evaluations resumed under per-episode locks.
- •
  2026-10-13, about 03:50 UTC: every author session began failing within
  seconds with a provider authorization error; the runtime recorded the
  empty deliveries as non-improving rounds. At 06:10 UTC, before j3’s
  exam score had been seen, the operator voided those rounds as
  infrastructure failures and returned each campaign to its state before
  the failure: j3’s R1.7, R1.8, C.7 and C.8 and j2’s I.6 were moved
  aside, not deleted, and the state change is recorded. j3 therefore
  resumed R1 after six repair rounds with one non-improving round; the
  exam that had been drawn when the failure stopped R1 was voided and
  j3’s exam was redrawn when R1 ended (R2_exam_2); j2’s three
  non-improving rounds were real sessions and its exam stood.
- •
  2026-10-14: j3’s ledger had grown to 3,876 rows and its final report
  exceeded the coordinator’s 600-second remote-command limit; an
  operator launcher that raises only that limit, with the runtime files
  and manifest untouched, produced the report and the held-out re-run.
- •
  j2’s isolation audit was graded review (another campaign’s directory
  name and identifiers appeared in process listings; no content read);
  the operator reviewed the events on 2026-10-14 and retained the
  campaign.

## Appendix F Result Files

Every campaign directory (data/protocol_A/\<campaign\>/ in the released
repository) holds fixed-schema files, one row per event, so that all
tables can be rebuilt by one script: campaign.json (scene, seed ranges,
limits, environment fingerprint, runtime manifest hash, official tree
hash); results/r2_gate_spec.json (the locked gate);
results/episodes.jsonl (hash-chained, one row per episode with stage,
mode, version, seed, outcome, failure class, safety events, primitive
calls, atom segments and coverage, decisions, times and cost);
results/measurement_draws.jsonl (exam, caller-check and re-evaluation
draws); state.json (R0, repair log, control versions, validation
checks); summary.json (outcome, compile cost, curves, gate checks,
caller check, control, isolation audit); held_out\_\*.json and
extra_eval\_\*.json (report-only re-runs); phase0_summary.json (the
health check and the expert runs). The frozen packages are released as
frozen_skills/\<task\>\_\<tag\>/ (the three frozen files and the
manifest). A reuse evaluation (data/protocol_B/\<evaluation\>/) writes
reuse_summary.json and decisions.jsonl (one row per caller decision with
tokens, price, latency and raw response) beside its ledger. The numbers
in this paper are produced by one script (analysis/paper/) from these
files and from the per-campaign analysis tables (analysis/data/); the
published values in
[Table 10](#S7.T10 "In 7.8 Caller check, audit, and the episode ledger ‣ 7 Results ‣ Compile Once, Run Cheap:Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents,and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds")
come from a transcription file (analysis/data/f09_reference.json,
checked against the PDF of arXiv:2506.18088v2) and the phase-0 expert
column from each campaign’s phase0_summary.json.
